passage: Deepika's future mother-in-law arrived at the Pune flat with sweets and a folded sheet of paper. "We ask for nothing, beta," she said warmly. "This is only custom. A sofa set, an air conditioner, a hall for five hundred guests, and gold for the bride, whatever you can manage." Deepika's father stared at his tea. Deepika read the sheet twice, her ears hot. Her younger brother Hrithik, home from his hostel, said in a low voice, "Papa, this is a list. That's dowry, and it's against the law." The visitor laughed lightly. "Such big words for a small tradition." Deepika folded the paper and handed it back. "Aunty, we're grateful you came. But we can't accept a list. Let's talk about the wedding without one." Her father's shoulders loosened, just slightly.

qa.q: What items were on the sheet?
qa.a: The sheet listed a sofa set, an air conditioner, a hall for five hundred guests and gold for the bride.

qa.q: How does Deepika feel as she reads the sheet twice?
qa.a: She feels angry and embarrassed. Her ears go hot because she can see that the "custom" is really a demand, yet she stays polite.

qa.q: Which choice did Deepika make when she handed the paper back?
qa.a: She thanked the visitor but refused a list and asked to plan the wedding without one, saying no without insulting anyone.

qa.q: How might Deepika's father feel when she declines?
qa.a: Probably relieved. His shoulders loosen slightly, and his earlier silence over his tea suggests he felt stuck until Deepika said what he could not.

grounding: A bride's family is told there is no demand, only custom, yet a list of items and a large wedding is expected, and it is recognised as dowry and refused.

passage: "They said nothing is needed," Papa said, folding the newspaper. "Only a hall for four hundred, a car for the couple, and gold as per custom. That's just how it is." "Papa, that is a demand," said Ritu, her voice shaking. "If nothing is needed, why is there a list?" "Suresh-uncle down the road did the same, and his daughter is happy." "Maybe she is. We don't have to copy anyone." Ritu swallowed. "It's dowry, Papa. It's against the law, and it starts my marriage with a price." Her mother set down a cup. "Madhav, drink your tea." Papa looked at the fan for a long time. "I don't want you to suffer." "I won't suffer for saying no. Let me speak to Rohan first. If he wants me only with a car, better to know now." Papa sighed. "Tell your mother. We'll ask them together."

qa.q: What did Papa say the list asked for?
qa.a: Papa said the list asked for a hall for four hundred, a car for the couple and gold as per custom.

qa.q: What is Ritu feeling when her voice shakes?
qa.a: Ritu feels nervous and angry but determined. She is afraid of upsetting her father, yet she cannot accept a marriage that starts with a price.

qa.q: What turning point comes when Ritu says she will speak to Rohan first?
qa.a: Ritu shifts from arguing to a concrete step, asking to speak to Rohan so the family can learn whether the demand is really his. Papa then agrees to ask together.

qa.q: How does Papa see the situation?
qa.a: Papa is afraid that Ritu will suffer and thinks copying Suresh-uncle is the safe path. After staring at the fan he softens and agrees to ask together.

grounding: A bride's family hears that nothing is demanded while a list of items and a lavish wedding is expected, and the daughter names it as dowry.

passage: You want to know why we borrowed? My name is Farida, and I'm Ishita's mother. When they asked for "a little gift" for her wedding, I said yes before my husband finished his tea. What if her in-laws were unkind to her? What if this proposal went and no one else came? So we borrowed from relatives and from the society, and paid for the hall, the furniture and the gold. My husband stopped sleeping. Two years on we are still paying, and a remark about "not enough" still comes now and then. I don't say it was foolish; it was love and fear. But I've thought: if five or six families in our lane had said no together, none of us would have borrowed. Now I tell my young neighbour Nazia: ask early, and ask together.

qa.q: What did Farida and her husband pay for?
qa.a: They paid for the hall, the furniture and the gold, using money borrowed from relatives and from the society.

qa.q: What was Farida afraid of when she said yes so quickly?
qa.a: Farida was afraid that her daughter's in-laws would be unkind to her and that no other proposal would come. Love and fear pushed her to agree.

qa.q: What turning point does Farida describe in her thinking, and what does she do about it?
qa.a: She realised that if several families in the lane had said no together, nobody would have borrowed. Now she tells her young neighbour Nazia to ask early and ask together.

qa.q: How was Farida's husband affected by the borrowing?
qa.a: He stopped sleeping, which shows the strain and worry it put on him.

grounding: A bride's mother agrees to demands and borrows heavily from fear for her daughter, and later sees that many families saying no together would change things.

passage: I live two doors from Uday, so I saw a lot last spring. First the tempo delivering a fridge and a bed, then the bank man visiting twice, then Uday selling the small plot behind the house. At the tea stall he kept telling everyone, "My Rani will be comfortable, that's all I want." He smiled every time, but he stopped ordering his usual second cup and left early. His wife Sushila carried boxes of sweets around the lane with her head high. On the wedding day Uday held his daughter for a long time. I can't say what was in his head. Maybe fear of a bad ending for Rani. Whatever it was, it cost him the plot. Four families in our lane did the same that year. Kunal

qa.q: What did Uday sell?
qa.a: Uday sold the small plot behind the house.

qa.q: What might Uday be feeling when he smiles but leaves the tea stall early, and how sure can Kunal be?
qa.a: Uday may be worried and strained under the smile, though Kunal cannot be sure. It is only a guess from the missing second cup and the early exits.

qa.q: Which choice did Uday make to secure Rani's comfort, and what did it cost him?
qa.a: He borrowed from a bank and sold the small plot behind the house, hoping to make sure Rani would be comfortable.

qa.q: How does Sushila seem to carry herself, and what might that show?
qa.a: She carries sweets around the lane with her head high. It might be pride, or it might cover worry, and Kunal cannot tell which.

grounding: A bride's parents take on debt and sell property to meet expectations out of love and fear for their daughter, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Rain was coming down when Bhupen reached his sister Charu's in-laws' colony, so he waited under the vegetable seller's tarpaulin as she had asked, because her mother-in-law checked her phone. Charu came out with a plastic bag, her hair wet, and spoke fast. Eight months married, and every week a new demand. "Your father promised a scooter." "Did your family send nothing for Diwali?" Last night her husband had said the demand was small if she loved him. "It's not my fault, is it, Bhaiya?" Bhupen lowered his umbrella over her. "It isn't. What they're doing is harassment, not tradition. I'm here. Tomorrow we'll go to Bua, and then to the legal aid centre, and you decide each step." Charu nodded, and let the rain hide her tears.

qa.q: Where did Bhupen wait for Charu?
qa.a: Bhupen waited under the vegetable seller's tarpaulin, as Charu had asked.

qa.q: What does Charu's question "It's not my fault, is it?" show about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels guilty and afraid that she is to blame, and lonely. Hiding her tears in the rain shows how hurt she is.

qa.q: What choice did Bhupen make in his answer that helped Charu?
qa.a: He believed her, said it was not her fault and named it harassment. He offered help while letting Charu decide each step.

qa.q: What might Bhupen be feeling as he listens under the tarpaulin?
qa.a: He is probably worried and protective, but he stays steady. Lowering his umbrella over her shows he wants her to feel safe.

grounding: A wife faces repeated demands and taunts after the wedding, and her family makes clear that it is harassment and offers trusted and legal support.

passage: Sabina's mother-in-law had a new remark for every meal. "Your family gave so little, no wonder..." That Saturday it was a demand: fifty thousand for her brother-in-law's shop, "as your family's share". Sabina's hands shook as she cleared the plates. From the balcony she rang her old college friend Nirmala, who worked at a legal aid centre in the city. "It isn't your fault, and it isn't custom," Nirmala said. "Write down the dates and what was said. Not to fight tonight, just so it's clear. And tell one person you trust, so you're not carrying it alone." That night Sabina wrote three months of dates in a small notebook. On Sunday she took the bus to Nirmala's office, where a counsellor listened for an hour without once asking what she had done to deserve it.

qa.q: What did Sabina's mother-in-law demand that Saturday?
qa.a: She demanded fifty thousand for her brother-in-law's shop, "as your family's share".

qa.q: How does Sabina feel as she clears the plates that Saturday?
qa.a: She feels frightened and hurt. Her hands shake, and she needs to step onto the balcony to call someone she trusts.

qa.q: Which choice by Sabina led to real support?
qa.a: Sabina rang her old college friend Nirmala, wrote down the dates in a notebook and went to the legal aid centre, where a counsellor listened to her.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel hearing Sabina's call?
qa.a: Probably concerned and steady. Nirmala calmly says it is not Sabina's fault and gives practical steps, showing care without panic.

grounding: A wife faces repeated demands and taunts about what her family gave, and gets help from a trusted friend and legal support.

passage: Bhavna, you asked how I knew to act when your neighbour's bride went quiet. I am Himani, and I was twenty-six when I noticed it in the flat next door. Kamla had been married four months. She stopped coming to the terrace, her phone was always with her mother-in-law, and once I heard her say, "I'll ask my father again." My stomach knotted. I did not knock on their door and accuse anyone. I brought her tea when her mother-in-law was out and simply said, "I'm here, and I won't judge." After three weeks she told me it was money her family was being pressed for. I said it was not her fault and gave her the number of a women's helpline, and I sat beside her while she called. The counsellor there listened for an hour. I kept visiting every week.

qa.q: How long had Kamla been married when Himani noticed the change?
qa.a: Kamla had been married four months.

qa.q: How did young Himani feel when she noticed Kamla going quiet?
qa.a: Himani was worried and uneasy. Himani's stomach knotted, though Himani stayed calm and did not accuse anyone.

qa.q: What choice did young Himani make instead of confronting the family?
qa.a: Himani brought Kamla tea when Kamla's mother-in-law was out and said there would be no judging, then kept visiting every week, so Kamla could open up in her own time.

qa.q: How might Kamla have felt when Himani said "I'm here, and I won't judge"?
qa.a: Probably relieved and a little safer. After three weeks Kamla shared the truth about the money her family was pressed for.

grounding: A neighbour notices a wife withdrawn, watched and pressed about money from her family, listens without judgement, keeps in touch and points her to a helpline.

passage: Akash had six minutes. Baljeet's mother-in-law had gone into the temple across the road, and Baljeet, whom he had known since college, stood at the stationery shop with her phone switched off and her eyes on the door. Over the last months she had stopped replying to messages. The one time he asked how she was, she said, "Money is tight for them, and my mother-in-law says my family owes a lot." Now he bought two pens so he'd look busy. "I won't ask anything," he said. "I'm not judging. My sister saved a helpline number for women, and here's mine, if you want to talk or just have tea." Baljeet slid the folded note into her bag. When the temple bell rang, she gave the smallest smile. Three days later a text arrived: "Thank you for the pens."

qa.q: How many minutes did Akash have?
qa.a: Akash had six minutes.

qa.q: What is Akash feeling as he buys two pens and talks to Baljeet?
qa.a: Akash is worried and careful. He buys pens to look busy, says he will not ask or judge, and keeps it short so Baljeet is not put at risk.

qa.q: Which choice by Akash kept the door open for Baljeet?
qa.a: He did not push for details or judge. He gave Baljeet a helpline number and his own number, and offered tea, so contact stayed possible.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel when she reads the folded note later?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone. The small smile and the text "Thank you for the pens" suggest she felt safely noticed.

grounding: A friend sees a woman withdrawn, watched and blamed about money from her family, listens without judgement, keeps contact and points her to helpline support.

passage: At the community centre office in Nashik, the booking clerk waited with the register while the family settled the plan for Naveen's cousin Omkar's wedding. Omkar's father read from a paper: "Groom's side wants a car, and the bride's family will cover the hall and the gold, as usual." Naveen, twenty-four, cleared his throat, his palms damp. "Uncle, may I say something? I don't think we should ask for any of it. It puts weight on the girl's family, and it's dowry, whatever we call it." The room went quiet. Naveen kept his voice level. "I'm only asking that we drop the list." Omkar's grandfather, Dada, tapped his stick. "The boy is right. In my time we refused too, and nothing collapsed." Omkar's father looked at the register, then folded the paper. "Let us talk again tonight."

qa.q: Where was the family settling the wedding plan?
qa.a: The family was at the community centre office in Nashik.

qa.q: What is Naveen feeling as he speaks up?
qa.a: Naveen is nervous but resolved. His palms are damp, yet he keeps his voice level and asks only that the list be dropped.

qa.q: What turning point came after Naveen spoke?
qa.a: Dada backed him, saying the boy was right and that nothing collapsed when they refused before, and Omkar's father folded the paper and agreed to talk again.

qa.q: How does Dada seem to see Naveen's speech?
qa.a: Dada sees it as right and worth supporting. His tapping stick and his words about refusing in his own time show he has held the same view quietly.

grounding: A relative objects calmly to a dowry list at the wedding-planning stage and finds support from an elder.

passage: Subject: About the list Dear Varun, I have been thinking since Sunday's planning call, and I would rather write than argue on the phone. The list sent to the bride's family, with the car, the cash "for the function" and the jewellery, is dowry, even if nobody says the word. I know you didn't write it, and I know they mean well. I'm not angry with anyone. But I don't want Meera's parents to borrow for us, and I don't want your marriage to begin with a price. I spoke to Dadi, and she said quietly that she never liked the custom either. She is willing to talk to Chachaji this week. Will you say something too? One more voice will make it easier for everyone. With love, Disha

qa.q: Who did Disha speak to about the list?
qa.a: Disha spoke to Dadi, who said she never liked the custom either.

qa.q: What is Disha feeling as she writes this email?
qa.a: Disha feels concerned but calm. Disha says nobody is being blamed and chose to write rather than argue on the phone.

qa.q: Which choice did Disha make that might help the change happen?
qa.a: Disha wrote calmly at the planning stage, spoke to Dadi first to find an ally and asked Varun to add his voice.

qa.q: How might Varun feel on reading the email?
qa.a: Probably caught between his parents and his conscience. Disha writes that she knows Varun did not write the list, which lets him listen without feeling attacked.

grounding: A relative objects to dowry calmly at the planning stage, finds an ally among the elders and asks another voice to join.

passage: "Amma, can I hold Meera's baby doll?" Eshaan whispered at his cousin's house. Lavanya glanced round. Two aunties were watching. "Of course, beta. What will you call her?" "Chhoti. She's hungry." He tucked the doll in the crook of his arm and rocked her, careful of her head. A cousin snorted, "Boys don't play with dolls!" Lavanya answered lightly, "Boys can be daddies too. Chhoti is lucky." Eshaan looked up and grinned, then went back to feeding the doll with a pretend bottle.

qa.q: What did Eshaan call the doll?
qa.a: Eshaan called the doll Chhoti.

qa.q: What might Eshaan feel when Lavanya says Chhoti is lucky?
qa.a: He probably feels happy and safe, since he grins and goes back to feeding the doll. 😊

qa.q: What choice did Lavanya make when the cousin snorted, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She answered lightly that boys can be daddies too instead of scolding or laughing. That let Eshaan keep playing without feeling ashamed.

qa.q: How might the cousin who snorted be affected by Lavanya's answer?
qa.a: The cousin may be a little surprised, since nobody shouted. The cousin may also learn that boys can care for babies.

grounding: A parent sees a boy wanting a doll and reacts calmly, so the child can play without shame.

passage: Note home, Thursday. Dear Damini's family, at outdoor play today Damini asked for the cricket bat, and four boys said, "That's not for girls." I stayed near. Damini said, "I want a turn," and held out her hand. I gave her the bat and stood beside her for the first swing. She missed twice and hit the third with a big laugh. The boys watched. Afterwards I told the whole group that everyone gets a turn with the bat and the skipping rope. Damini has asked for the bat again tomorrow. Elizabeth, class teacher 🙂

qa.q: How many times did Damini miss before she hit the ball?
qa.a: Damini missed twice and hit the third one with a big laugh.

qa.q: What might Damini be feeling when she holds out her hand and says "I want a turn"?

qa.q: What choice did Elizabeth make that let Damini play?
qa.a: Elizabeth waited and watched first, then gave Damini the bat and stood beside her for the first swing, and later told the whole group everyone gets turns.

qa.q: How might the boys have been affected by watching Damini?
qa.a: They watched quietly and heard that everyone gets turns, so they may learn that the bat is not only for boys.

grounding: An adult watches a girl who wants the cricket bat and responds calmly so that she can play.

passage: In the Kraków flat, Sunday lunch was over. Paula's mother stacked the plates. "Paula, come and dry these, please." Paula looked at the sofa. Her brother Marek, twelve, was already stretched out with his tablet, one sock hanging off the armrest. Nobody called him. Paula took the towel. The water ran warm, and forks clattered in the sink. She counted the plates as she dried them: fourteen. Through the doorway she could hear the cheering of a game. She did not say anything. She dried the last cup very slowly and set it on the shelf, then looked at the towel in her hand, wet all the way through.

qa.q: How many plates did Paula count?
qa.a: Paula counted fourteen plates.

qa.q: What might Paula be feeling as she dries the last cup very slowly?
qa.a: She is probably resentful and tired. She notices that nobody called Marek, yet she says nothing.

qa.q: What choice did Paula make about speaking up, and what else could be tried?
qa.a: Paula stayed silent and dried slowly. She could calmly ask whether Marek can dry the next round, or her mother could call both children.

qa.q: How might Marek see the afternoon?
qa.a: He may not notice anything unfair, since nobody called him and he is absorbed in his game.

grounding: A girl is asked to help in the kitchen while her brother plays, and she notices the difference without saying a word.

passage: At the Diwali fair at the community centre, Uma, nine, was sent to the kitchen counter to help make puris. Her brother Ravi, eleven, was allowed to go and play carrom with the boys in the hall. Uma rolled out puris beside two other girls while the carrom coins clacked in the next room. She said nothing but looked at the doorway twice. Charu, the volunteer in charge of the kitchen rota, noticed. She wiped her hands. "Helpers, everyone washes hands and comes to the counter, boys and girls. Ravi, come, you're on laddus." Ravi groaned, then shaped one lopsided laddu and glanced at Uma as if to check. Uma pressed a puri flat and half smiled.

qa.q: What was Ravi allowed to do in the hall?
qa.a: Ravi was allowed to play carrom with the boys in the hall.

qa.q: What is Uma likely feeling as she looks at the doorway twice?
qa.a: Uma probably feels left out and a little resentful, though she says nothing.

qa.q: What turning point came when Charu spoke?
qa.a: Charu called all helpers, boys and girls, to the counter and put Ravi on laddus, so the work was shared and Uma no longer worked alone.

qa.q: Why might Charu have stepped in?
qa.a: Charu noticed Uma's glances at the doorway and saw that the work was unevenly split, so she changed the rota.

grounding: A girl is sent to work in the kitchen while her brother plays, and notices the unfairness without words until an adult shares the tasks.

passage: Salma: Abbu says his daughter must be home by six. Wasim gets to stay out till ten. Wasim: I heard. Salma: "It's for your safety." Then why does it feel like he doesn't trust me 😠 Wasim: He's scared, Salma. But you're right, it's not the same rule for both of us. Salma: Half of me feels looked after. Half feels like a suspect. Wasim: Which road actually worries him? The one by the tea shop is dark. Salma: The lane after the tuition centre. I'd take the main road if he said that's fine. Wasim: Let's talk to him tonight. Maybe six-thirty, share location, and I text him when I'm out too. Same rules for both. Salma: That last part might actually work. Thanks bhai 🙂

qa.a: Abbu says Salma must be home by six.

qa.q: What does Salma mean by "half of me feels looked after, half feels like a suspect"?
qa.a: She feels protected by the care but distrusted by the rule. Both feelings are real at once.

qa.q: What turning point in the chat makes a fairer plan possible?
qa.a: Wasim asks which road really worries Abbu, so they can talk about actual risks and propose a shared rule, with location sharing and texts from both.

qa.q: How does Wasim see the different curfews?
qa.a: Wasim sees that Abbu is scared and means well, but he admits it is not the same rule for both and offers to follow the same one. 🙂

grounding: A teenage girl must be home by dark while her brother comes and goes freely, feels both protected and distrusted, and finds that open talk about real risks helps.

passage: In their village near Satara, the temple bell rang at dusk, and Sujata, fifteen, was already walking home from the tuition class while her brother Omkar, seventeen, cycled towards the cricket ground. At the door Baba said as usual, "The road gets dark, and people talk. It's for your safety." Sujata felt warmed by his worry and stung by it at once. "Baba, I know you worry. But Omkar is out past nine and I can't walk home at six?" Omkar, who had come back for his bat, said, "The stretch by the sugar mill has no light. That's the real problem." Baba looked at his son, then at his daughter. "Show me the road tomorrow." They walked it together at dusk, and afterwards agreed on the same rule for both when it's dark, and that Omkar would ride Sujata back from class.

qa.q: Where does the story take place?
qa.a: It takes place in their village near Satara.

qa.q: How does Sujata feel when Baba says it is for her safety?
qa.a: She feels warmed by his worry and stung by it at once, protected and distrusted together.

qa.q: What turning point led to a fairer rule?
qa.a: Omkar named the real problem, the unlit stretch by the sugar mill, and Baba agreed to walk the road with them, which led to the same rule for both.

qa.q: What might Baba be thinking as he looks at his son, then at his daughter?
qa.a: He may be realising that his rule treats his children differently and that his real fear is the dark road, so he chooses to see it for himself.

grounding: A teenage girl must be home by dark while her brother comes and goes freely, feels protected and distrusted, and open talk about the real risks produces a fair rule.

passage: Ganga, you asked why your father tells such jokes when he is sad, so sit and listen. I am Minakshi, your Dadi. When your father Ravi was fourteen, his team lost the kabaddi final, and he came home with red eyes. His father said, "Boys don't cry. Wipe your face." Ravi did. By evening he was doing the referee's voice for everyone, and by night he snapped at his sister for touching his shoes. I saw that the jokes were a lid. That night I sat beside him on the stairs and said nothing for a long time. Then I said, "I cried for days when my own grandmother died. It's allowed." Ravi's shoulders dropped and he cried against my arm. His father, in the doorway, said nothing that night. The next morning he brought Ravi his tea himself.

qa.q: What happened at the kabaddi final?
qa.a: Ravi's team lost the kabaddi final, and he came home with red eyes.

qa.q: How did Ravi feel after being told "Boys don't cry", and how could Minakshi tell?
qa.a: Ravi felt sad and probably ashamed of it. He hid it behind jokes and then snapped at his sister, which Minakshi saw as a lid.

qa.q: What choice did Minakshi make that night that helped Ravi?
qa.a: She sat beside him quietly for a long time instead of scolding, then told him she had cried for days too and that it was allowed.

qa.q: How might Ravi's father have felt watching from the doorway?
qa.a: Probably unsettled and thoughtful, since he said nothing and the next morning he brought Ravi tea himself.

grounding: A boy is told to be strong and stop crying, hides sadness behind jokes and anger, and is helped by someone who lets him be sad.

passage: The house was full of relatives for the thirteenth-day rites, and there was no quiet corner anywhere. Tarun, fifteen, had not cried once since his grandfather died. "You're the eldest grandson now, be strong, no tears," an uncle told him. Tarun laughed too loudly and did impressions of the priest for the cousins. When his older cousin Jomon asked, "You okay?" Tarun snapped, "Why wouldn't I be? Leave it." Jomon didn't argue. Later, on the crowded terrace stairs, Jomon sat down two steps below him with two cups of tea. "I cried in the bathroom for an hour when my nana died," Jomon said. "No one heard." Tarun stared at the cup. Then his shoulders shook, and Jomon kept sitting there.

qa.q: Who told Tarun to be strong and shed no tears?
qa.a: An uncle told him to be strong, with no tears.

qa.q: Why did Tarun snap at Jomon, and what was Tarun feeling underneath?
qa.a: Tarun snapped because the question came too close to the grief he was hiding. Underneath he felt sad and overwhelmed.

qa.q: What choice did Jomon make on the stairs that changed the moment?
qa.a: Jomon sat down quietly with tea and shared crying in the bathroom too, without pushing, so Tarun could let go.

qa.q: How might Jomon see Tarun's jokes and anger?
qa.a: Jomon may see them as a way of covering grief, so Jomon does not argue but waits for a quieter moment.

grounding: A boy is told to be strong and stop crying, hides sadness behind jokes and anger, and is helped by someone who shares their own tears.

passage: Counsellor's note, Friday. Vijay, 21, a final-year student, came in after his father Wasim told him to accept the highest-paying job on offer, an office role he dreads. Vijay wants to become a school science teacher. He said, "Papa says a man has to earn well, and teaching won't do." I noted his flat voice and clenched hands. I asked if he would like me to meet his father with him. On Wednesday the three of us sat together. Wasim explained that he had struggled with money in his own youth and did not want that for his son. Vijay described the work he loves. Wasim asked what a teacher's first-year pay looks like and said he would think about it. I will see Vijay again next week.

qa.q: What job did Vijay's father want him to accept?
qa.a: Vijay's father wanted him to accept the highest-paying job on offer, an office role.

qa.q: What is Vijay feeling when he says "teaching won't do"?
qa.a: Vijay feels dismissed and tense. His flat voice and clenched hands suggest he is holding back frustration about being pushed into a mould.

qa.q: Which choice by Vijay opened the way to real family support?
qa.a: Vijay agreed to have the counsellor meet his father with him, so both could speak honestly and Wasim could hear the work Vijay loves.

qa.q: Why might Wasim have pushed for the highest-paying job?
qa.a: Wasim struggled with money in his own youth and did not want that for his son. His push comes from care, and he was willing to think again.

grounding: A young man is told to earn well rather than follow the work he loves, and real choice opens when his family listens with support.

passage: Tuesday night. Amma and Papa had a family talk at dinner. For me: "Take a government clerk job near home, Jahnavi. Easy hours, good for marriage." Amma says a daughter's job should be easy. For my brother Shankar: "Leave your art course, do engineering and earn well, or no girl will look at you." Shankar has not eaten his rice. We sat on the stairs afterwards and he said, "They're fitting both of us into moulds." I said I want to try the data analyst training in Hyderabad. He said he wants to paint and teach art. We agreed to ask Amma and Papa for one honest conversation on Sunday, with Dadi there. I'm nervous. But it's the first time either of us said what we really want out loud. Jahnavi

qa.q: What job did Amma and Papa suggest for Jahnavi?
qa.a: They suggested a government clerk job near home, with easy hours.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi feel about the conversation planned for Sunday?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels nervous but also relieved, because saying what she and Shankar really want out loud was a first.

qa.q: Which choice by Jahnavi and Shankar on the stairs could make real choice possible?
qa.a: They decided to say what each of them wants and to ask their parents for one honest conversation on Sunday, with Dadi there.

qa.q: How might Shankar see what their parents want for him?
qa.a: Shankar sees it as a mould. He is expected to leave his art course, do engineering and earn well, and he was too upset to eat his rice.

grounding: A young woman is told to pick an easy job for marriage while her brother is told to earn well, and they decide to ask their family for an honest talk.
